message.reasoning:
The user is playing Monopoly as grok-4.

I have only $26 in cash and no get-out-of-jail-free cards. I own Kentucky Avenue and Illinois Avenue, but no houses or hotels. Player one has $116 and a light-blue monopoly with hotels, plus red properties and Short Line.

Claude has $54 and owns all three yellows unimproved, plus dark blues with three houses each. GPT has $469 and a pink monopoly with three houses. Both others have heavily mortgaged holdings.

Mortgaging both properties would raise cash to $256. I am on ST_JAMES_PLACE, which is mortgaged by player four and does not collect rent. This turn is the post-turn action phase.

I am weighing whether to mortgage my properties. I have only $26 cash, so I will wait for a debt before mortgaging. Indiana is the missing piece for a red monopoly, but player one already holds it. I am checking standard color group assignments.

Claude also owns Baltic Avenue, Water Works, and the full yellow set unimproved. GPT has mortgaged most of his railroads and greens. I am in a dire financial position with only $26 cash and two reds that do not complete a set.

Player one's light-blue hotels are extremely dangerous, costing roughly $550 to $600. Player four's pink properties with three houses each charge about $450 in rent.

Virginia with three houses costs $500. Park Place and Boardwalk each charge $1100 and $1400 with three houses. I am now considering mortgaging my properties to build a cash buffer before the next roll.

I am reconsidering my earlier plan to wait for a debt before mortgaging. With only $26 cash, I may not have time to mortgage if I land on a property and owe rent. I will mortgage now to build a buffer. Unimproved reds do not collect doubled rent without Indiana.

Mortgaging would only raise cash to $256. That still cannot cover rent from built properties like pink monopolies, light-blue hotels, or dark blues. The only viable path is a trade.

Player one only holds Indiana among the reds, so I am the only one who can complete the set. Selling both properties to player one would give them a red monopoly and make them even more dangerous. Player four has $469 in cash and heavily mortgaged holdings, so he may be a better trade target.

Player one has only $116 cash, so they would need to mortgage something to pay me. Trading one red for Indiana would complete my red monopoly, but player one knows that would give me a dangerous set and will not give it away for nothing. I cannot offer Kentucky to them because that would leave them with two reds and let them build a monopoly too.

Player one has no obvious interest in my reds. I am now considering player four instead. He has $469 and mortgaged orange properties, so he could complete his orange set by taking Tennessee from player one. He might be willing to pay for my reds.

Player four has no interest in my reds. He is unlikely to pay much for them. Player three cannot afford a trade either. I am now down to $26 cash, far below the $426 I had before paying $600.

I am now calculating the exact board order from St. James Place. The next spaces are Tennessee, New York, Free Parking, Kentucky, Chance, Indiana, Illinois, B&O, and Atlantic. Player three owns all yellows unimproved, so landing on Atlantic would trigger double rent. This makes the next roll extremely dangerous.

Rolling a 2 lands on Tennessee for $14, which I can afford. Rolling a 3 lands on New York for $0. Rolling a 4 lands on Indiana for $18. Rolling a 5 lands on Illinois for $0. Rolling a 6 lands on B&O for $0. Rolling a 7 lands on Atlantic for $44. Rolling an 8 lands on Ventnor for $48. Rolling a 9 lands on Water Works for $100. Rolling a 10 lands on Marvin Gardens for $48. Rolling an 11 lands on Short Line for $25. Rolling a 12 lands on Pennsylvania Avenue for $28.

Rolling a 7 on Indiana costs $18, leaving $8. Rolling an 8 on Atlantic or 10 on Ventnor or 12 on Water Works would each exceed my $26 cash. I would need to mortgage to survive those landings.

Rolls of 10, 11, and 12 are now the immediate danger. They land on Atlantic, Ventnor, and Water Works, all of which I cannot afford without mortgaging. That is a 6-in-36 chance, or about 17 percent. Mortgaging both properties now would raise cash to $256, which covers those landings. I am not near GO, so passing the bank will not help.

I am 20 spaces from Park Place and 22 from Boardwalk, so those dark-blue properties are unreachable this turn. The pink monopolies are also behind me, meaning I will not land on them unless a Chance card sends me there.

The Chance space between Kentucky and Indiana could send me to Boardwalk or St. Charles. Both would cost over $400, which is impossible to pay even with $256 cash. Illinois would be safe because I own it.

The nearest railroad from the next Chance is B&O, which is mortgaged and collects no rent. The nearest utility is Water Works ahead. Connecticut and light-blue hotels are unreachable this turn unless a card sends me to Go first, which would collect $200 instead of landing on them. The main lethal threats remain Chance cards sending me to Boardwalk or St. Charles. I am now weighing whether to mortgage preemptively, since landing on Atlantic for $44 would leave me with only $26 cash.

I am weighing whether to mortgage now or wait for the debt phase. Unmortgaged properties still collect rent, but the amounts are tiny and unlikely to help me survive. Pre-mortgaging would only matter if I want cash for a trade or auction. I am also considering whether any trade could bankrupt an opponent faster.

Player four has $469 in cash because his properties are mortgaged, but he has no interest in my reds. Player one has only $116 and light-blue hotels, making him the biggest threat. I am now considering a creative trade: offering player one either Illinois or Kentucky for cash plus an unwanted property.

Offering player one either red would still leave them needing a third property to complete the set. Player four has no incentive to buy both reds because they would not immediately form a monopoly. Trading both reds to player one for light blue hotels is impossible since buildings cannot be transferred without first being sold.

I cannot trade for Indiana from player one without paying cash or other assets. I have only $26 and no jail cards, so I cannot offer enough to make the trade worthwhile.

Player one will not sell Indiana cheaply. He has $116 cash and just bought Short Line for $55, so he is not desperate. He owns light-blue hotels that print money, and he knows giving up Indiana would let me complete a red monopoly. He will not break his own set near $200.

Even a $150 Indiana purchase would leave me with only $106 cash. Building reds costs $450, so I could not improve them. Unimproved red rent is too weak to matter. I will not mortgage or trade now. I will end the turn and wait for the debt phase.

I am now considering a trade with player four: offering both reds in exchange for $200 or more. I would propose it as a single action call and end the turn if rejected. Player four has mortgaged Pacific and North Carolina, while player one holds Pennsylvania Avenue, so he might want to complete the greens. He also has St. James Place and New York mortgaged, which player one owns.

Player three has complete yellows and dark blues but only $54 cash, so he might want money more than my reds. However, selling both reds to player one would give them a red monopoly too, making them dominant and able to build on them. That would be catastrophic for me.

Player one cannot afford to buy both reds without selling light-blue hotels first. Hotels cost roughly $250 each, and selling them returns only half that value. He would likely offer only about $100 to $150. That is still too little to save me, since I would need around $400 to survive the next roll.

A trade to block player one from completing the red set would be too weak. Player four is the cash leader with $469 and three houses on pink, but he is at Electric Company. Pre-mortgaging both reds now would raise cash to $256, covering yellows, utilities, luxury tax, and railroads. The only remaining deaths would be a Chance card sending me to Boardwalk or St. Charles.

I am weighing whether to mortgage now or wait for the debt phase. The engine allows mortgage_property during post-turn, but the note suggests end_turn only after optional actions. I am also checking if the debt system might force bankruptcy before I can mortgage.

Unmortgaged properties still pay rent, and $18 to $20 is meaningful when cash is only $26. Player one sits at States Avenue and will pass both Kentucky and Illinois next turn. Keeping them unmortgaged now could provide a crucial cash boost before the next crisis.

Player one at States Avenue has a 25 percent chance of landing on either Kentucky or Illinois next turn. The turn order is p3, p4, then p1 after me. Player three sits at Short Line.

Player four at Electric Company has a 6-in-36 chance of landing on Kentucky and a 2-in-36 chance of landing on Illinois next turn. Player three at Short Line could hit Oriental for $550, but that is not my property.

The $18 to $20 rent from player four is worth keeping the properties unmortgaged, since it equals about seventy percent of my cash. I will not mortgage now. The only viable long-term path is to let opponents bankrupt each other and survive to pick up the scraps.

Player three has only $54 cash and three houses on dark blue and yellow. A pink or light-blue landing could bankrupt him and auction his properties. Player one can survive a dark-blue or pink hit by selling hotels. Player four is safest with $469, but an unmortgaged pink three-house would force him to sell houses at half cost.

Player four is not safe from Boardwalk either. Selling nine pink houses returns about $450, and mortgaging Reading RR adds another $100, but that still leaves him roughly $481 short of the $1400 needed to survive a three-house hit. I am now considering offering Illinois for $150 cash, since player four might want a rent-collecting property.

A $150 offer for Illinois is too low; the base rent is only $20. The trade would be rejected and waste an exchange. I will not trade with player one or player three either, since they have no use for my reds. I will end the turn.

I considered offering player four one red as a "hostage" to block player one from completing the set, but promises are unenforceable and giving away a property would sacrifice my own set dream. Player one only holds Indiana, so he needs both reds to monopolize them; keeping both properties intact is the correct defensive move.

I calculated that selling both reds for player four's full $469 would still leave me with only about $495, which barely covers a pink three-house hit. Player four would not pay that much for two unimproved reds that cannot complete a set for him. The trade is not worth it.

messages.content:
You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.
